title: Rent (musical)
description: American rock musical by Jonathan Larson
wiki_lead:
Rent (stylized in all caps) is a rock musical with music, lyrics, and book by Jonathan Larson. Loosely based on the 1896 opera La bohème by Giacomo Puccini, Luigi Illica, and Giuseppe Giacosa, it tells the story of a group of impoverished young artists struggling to survive and create a life in Lower Manhattan's East Village, in the thriving days of the bohemian culture of Alphabet City, under the shadow of HIV/AIDS.
The musical was first seen in 1993 in a workshop production at New York Theatre Workshop, the off-Broadway theatre which was also where the musical began performances on January 26, 1996. The show's creator, Jonathan Larson, had died suddenly of an aortic dissection the night before. The musical moved to Broadway's larger Nederlander Theatre on April 29, 1996.
On Broadway, Rent gained critical acclaim and won several awards, including the Pulitzer Prize for Drama and the Tony Award for Best Musical. The Broadway production closed on September 7, 2008, after 12 years, making it one of the longest-running shows on Broadway. The production grossed over $280 million.
The success of the show led to several national tours and numerous foreign productions. In 2005, it was adapted into a motion picture featuring six of the eight principal cast members from the 1996 stage premiere.

Concept and genesis
In 1988, playwright Billy Aronson wanted to create "a musical based on Puccini's La Bohème, in which the luscious splendor of Puccini's world would be replaced with the coarseness and noise of modern New York." In 1989, Jonathan Larson, a 29-year-old composer, began collaborating with Aronson on this project, and the two composed together "Santa Fe", "Rent", and "I Should Tell You". Larson suggested setting the play "in the East Village neighborhood of Manhattan." He suggested making "Rent" the title; Aronson agreed. In 1991, he asked Aronson if he could use Aronson's original concept and make Rent his own. Larson had ambitious expectations for Rent; his ultimate dream was to write a rock opera "to bring musical theater to the MTV generation". Aronson and Larson made an agreement that if the show went to Broadway, Aronson would share in the proceeds and be given credit for "original concept & additional lyrics".
Jonathan Larson focused on composing Rent in the early 1990s, waiting tables at the Moondance Diner to support himself. Over the course of years, Larson wrote hundreds of songs and made many drastic changes to the show, which in its final incarnation contained 42 songs. In the fall of 1992, Larson approached James Nicola, artistic director of New York Theatre Workshop, with a tape and copy of Rent's script. When Rent had its first staged reading at New York Theatre Workshop in March 1993, it became evident that, despite its very promising material and moving musical numbers, many structural problems needed to be addressed, including its cumbersome length and overly complex plot.

grok_lead: Rent is a rock musical with book, music, and lyrics by Jonathan Larson, centering on a group of bohemian artists, performers, and intellectuals in New York City's East Village confronting poverty, addiction, and the HIV/AIDS epidemic in the era before effective treatments. The show premiered off-Broadway at the Nederlander Theatre 's WPA Theatre on January 25, 1996, the day after Larson's sudden death from an aortic dissection at age 35, which garnered significant media attention and propelled its rapid transfer to Broadway on April 29, 1996, at the Nederlander Theatre. Loosely inspired by Puccini's opera La BohÃ¨me, Rent updates the narrative to modern-day Manhattan, emphasizing themes of love, community, and defiance against societal marginalization through its score of energetic rock anthems, including the hit " Seasons of Love." The production achieved unprecedented commercial and critical success, running for 5,123 performances and becoming the eighth-longest-running show in Broadway history, while winning the 1996 Pulitzer Prize for Drama and the Tony Award for Best Musical, among other honors. Despite its acclaim as a generational touchstone that raised awareness of the AIDS crisis, Rent has faced retrospective criticisms for romanticizing urban poverty and bohemian lifestyles, perpetuating stereotypes of marginalized communities, and presenting an overly optimistic view of HIV/AIDS that some argue glosses over the epidemic's harsher realities and institutional failures. A 2005 film adaptation directed by Chris Columbus underperformed at the box office and received mixed reviews for failing to capture the stage production's vitality.
